lesson.title: How Big Is It, Really? Peak, Peak-to-Peak, and RMS Amplitude
lesson.summary: Amplitude describes how large a signal's swing is, but circuits work actually uses several distinct amplitude measures, peak, peak-to-peak, and RMS, that describe the same wave in different ways, and mixing them up is a common source of factor of 2 or factor of 1.41 errors.
lesson.body:
For a simple sinusoid v(t) = Vp sin(omega t + theta), amplitude most strictly means Vp, the peak value measured from the signal's center line up to its highest point. In everyday circuits language, though, several related numbers all get called amplitude loosely: peak amplitude (Vp), peak-to-peak amplitude (Vpp = 2 Vp, measured from the very top of the wave to the very bottom), and RMS amplitude (Vrms = Vp divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707 Vp), which is the effective value used for power calculations. All three describe the same wave; they just answer different questions about it.

The distinction is not academic. An oscilloscope trace is usually easiest to read as peak-to-peak, since that is the vertical distance directly visible between the highest and lowest points on the grid. A wall outlet rating like 120 V or 230 V is always an RMS value, not a peak value. A datasheet's stated output swing is usually peak-to-peak. Treating one of these as if it were another produces errors of a factor of 2 (confusing peak with peak-to-peak) or a factor of about 1.41 (confusing peak with RMS), both common and both avoidable once you are explicit about which amplitude you mean.

Here is a fully worked example that ties amplitude together with the DC component and AC component from the previous two chapters. Consider v(t) = 5 V + 15 sin(omega t - 30 degrees). The DC component is 5 V, the constant offset, or center line, of the whole signal. The AC component is the 15 sin(omega t - 30 degrees) term, whose peak amplitude is 15 V. Its peak-to-peak amplitude is 2 times 15 = 30 V (a DC offset shifts a waveform up or down but never changes its peak-to-peak swing). Its RMS amplitude is 15 divided by the square root of 2, about 10.6 V. Now find the actual maximum and minimum of the full signal directly: the maximum occurs when the sine term equals +1, giving v_max = 5 + 15 = 20 V; the minimum occurs when the sine term equals -1, giving v_min = 5 - 15 = -10 V. As a check, the peak-to-peak swing computed this way is 20 - (-10) = 30 V, matching the 2 times 15 V figure exactly. So this single signal is fully described as a 5 V DC level with a 15 V peak (30 V peak-to-peak, 10.6 V RMS) sinusoidal AC component riding on top of it, producing a waveform that swings from -10 V up to +20 V.

One closing point worth carrying forward: for a non-sinusoidal periodic waveform, there is no single number that is simply the amplitude the way there is for a pure sinusoid. As the Harmonic Content and Spectrum chapters showed, each individual harmonic in the Fourier series has its own amplitude Cn at its own frequency. The habit worth building here is always being specific: amplitude of what, peak or peak-to-peak or RMS, and of which component, the whole signal, its AC component alone, or one particular harmonic.
